process.text: I take things apart until I understand them. Then I put them back together until they feel right.

for.text: Offpriced, a Montréal stocklot house selling clothing by the lot to retailers and wholesalers buying surplus, cancelled orders and factory over-runs in bulk.

oneLine.text: One app for buyers, staff and editors — with a site the owner updates by talking to an AI.

facts.text: direct from fifty-seven factories, trade only
a single application serving four audiences: the public, signed-in buyers, the team working those deals, and whoever edits the site

problem.text: Deals were negotiated by email with no single record of what was promised, and because every lot is a one-off with no restock, a public site nobody in the business could edit quickly became stale and a liability.

built.text: The public site — a shop window centred on 'The Floor', the catalogue of lots currently available.
The buyer portal — line sheets, enquiries, quotes and orders tracked end to end instead of scattered across inboxes.
The internal operations app — a mobile-first CRM for staff to keep The Floor current and manage quotes and fulfilment.
The admin CMS, plus an MCP-based AI publishing flow so the owner can draft and publish articles by talking to Claude.

decisions.text: Embedded Payload CMS in the same Next.js codebase rather than running it as a second service, so there is one deployment and one login model instead of two systems to keep in sync.
Built the MCP server as a deliberately small, fixed set of actions behind a secret token, because the point was giving the AI assistant specific controls, not open access.
Modelled the sales lifecycle end to end with an automatic email and a permanent record at each transition, so a buyer dispute over a missed quote is a lookup, not an argument.
Segregated push notifications by audience, so an internal alert about a deal or a late shipment never reaches a customer's phone.
Fixed the design system — colour, type and spacing — before building any screens, so a new screen is assembly, not invention.

outcome.text: One system where there were several disconnected ones. Buyers self-serve instead of waiting on a reply, staff work deals from a phone, and the site is edited by the people who know what it should say. Every enquiry, quote and order has a trail. And the owner publishes by talking.

kind.text: a small ERP, built from scratch

for.cite: case-study-staffing.md:21 (client name withheld per naming rules)

oneLine.text: Five portals, one login, and every company's data walled off inside the database itself.

facts.text: five relationships at once — its own team, the client companies, the people it places, the recruiters who source them, and the prospects it chases
927 automated tests run against all of it.

problem.text: On spreadsheets, that produces the two failure modes that hurt: money that quietly leaks, and information reaching the wrong company. The requirement: one system, five doors into it, and doors that do not connect.

built.text: Five portals — Admin, Client, Worker, Partner, and an Onboarding flow that converts a prospect into a client once money changes hands.
Permissions through CASL, precise enough to say a person may approve a specific record, not just that they hold a role.
A workflow engine of state machines for approvals, so a request can't skip a step and changing a process happens in one place.
An invoicing engine on integer minor-currency units with one written rounding rule, and an append-only audit log.

decisions.text: Enforced tenant isolation as row-level security inside the database itself rather than in application code, because an application filter can be forgotten in one query and leak another company's payroll.
Ran ordinary traffic through a deliberately powerless database account that cannot switch the row-level security checks off; a separate privileged account exists only for maintenance.
Stored money as whole numbers of the smallest currency unit rather than binary floating point, because floating point cannot represent most money amounts exactly and the error accumulates.
Made the audit log append-only, so rewriting history takes deliberate action through the maintenance account rather than a quiet edit from inside the app.
Deliberately left out the codebase knowledge graph used on another project, because five portals over one shared core is a structure that fits in one person's head.

outcome.text: Five groups, one platform, each seeing only its own slice. Work approved once and billed from the same record, commissions calculated rather than reconstructed, a history that cannot be quietly rewritten.

walls.text: Each of the five portals connects into one shared core and one database; row-level security independently checks every read and write so one client company's rows cannot leak to another's.

kind.text: a website with one job — turn a tournament organiser or a brand's event manager into a booking enquiry

for.text: lucif3r, an esports caster, stage host and broadcast voice working across esports finals, brand launches and live conventions
for.cite: case-study-esports-talent.md:25 (source reads '[lucif3r](url) is an esports caster, stage host...'; name de-linked here)

oneLine.text: A booking site that feels like a live broadcast — kept current by the talent, not a developer.

facts.text: The audience was written down before anything was designed: tournament organisers and esports organisations first, then brand and event managers, then sponsors.
Success is measured in qualified enquiries, not pageviews.
a near-black ground, warm off-white type, one magenta accent, and gold kept for numbers and highlights

problem.text: Generic talent sites and link-in-bio pages don't sell a broadcaster, and the site needed to turn organisers, brand managers and sponsors into booking enquiries, with content the talent could keep current without a developer for each new event.

built.text: A broadcast-style design system — near-black ground, one magenta accent, gold for highlights, square corners by rule, and a film-grain texture layer.
Motion with a reduced-motion off switch: a glitching wordmark, a gold shimmer, a ticker, and smoothed scrolling.
A home page built around one path to the booking form, with a bento grid of past events and a gallery from the stage.
A custom Control Room on top of embedded Payload CMS, with live preview, draft/publish, and even the brand colours editable.

decisions.text: Kept all effects to plain CSS plus one small scrolling library, so nothing heavy has to download before the page comes alive.
Gave mobile its own layout rather than a squeezed desktop one, because a booking often starts with a link opened on a phone.
Settled the look through two HTML prototypes rather than debating directions, and removed a layered custom cursor once the grain layer supplied the same depth.
Validated the booking form in the browser and again on the server against the same rules, and used Cloudflare Turnstile to keep bots out.
Kept analytics and Speed Insights on the public site only, never inside the Control Room.

outcome.text: A site that looks like the job: broadcast energy from the first frame, proof of the stages already worked, and a booking form at the end of every path. It stays current because the talent keeps it current — new events, new photos, even new colours — without waiting on anyone.

kind.text: Real-Time NSE Market Monitoring on an Event-Driven Stack

oneLine.text: Roughly 800 live RSI streams, divergence alerts and MACD setups — computed as the market moves and streamed to the browser.

facts.text: around 200 NSE stocks on four intraday timeframes at once
Kafka 4.1 runs in KRaft mode — no ZooKeeper to operate
Every two seconds it reads the live board from Redis and pushes it to every connected client

problem.text: A divergence between price and RSI can form and dissolve within a quarter of an hour, and across roughly 200 stocks on four timeframes that is about 800 charts — more than anyone can watch by eye — so the watching had to move off the screen and into a system.

built.text: A live monitoring board showing RSI across four timeframes per stock, with divergence highlighting and search.
A divergence history view, filterable by stock, timeframe, type and confidence.
A MACD strategy view showing daily market bias and the setups and triggers that follow on shorter timeframes.
Accounts and subscriptions with phone-verified sign-up, Razorpay payments, and an admin console for users, payments and feedback.

decisions.text: Aligned candles to the 9:15 IST market open rather than the Unix clock, so a 15-minute candle on Tredye matches the one on a charting terminal.
Backfilled months of history on start-up before computing indicators, and gated the detectors behind a warm-up announcement on Kafka for up to half an hour.
Consolidated candle history onto PostgreSQL instead of the dedicated time-series database the original blueprint specified, to run one fewer datastore.
Put a single FastAPI gateway in front holding one WebSocket per browser, pushing the live board from Redis every two seconds rather than on every tick.
Compiled TA-Lib once in a shared Docker build stage, with each service built as a thin target on top of it.

outcome.text: Tredye keeps roughly 800 live RSI streams current through an event-driven pipeline and surfaces the patterns worth a second look while they still matter — on a phone or at a desk, from the opening bell to the close. Each stage runs in its own container, and subscriptions, payments and an admin console are built in.

line.text: Building full-stack web platforms for clients end to end — B2B commerce and CRM, multi-portal operations software and motion-led brand sites — with Next.js, Payload CMS and PostgreSQL.

Built "Tredye", a real-time market-monitoring platform for NSE stocks: Python services on Kafka, Redis and PostgreSQL, with a Next.js dashboard. Built the event-driven data pipeline, alerts and backtesting.
